clinician.final_diagnosis: Miller-Fisher Syndrome subtype presenting with isolated bilateral mydriasis
clinician.trajectory_summary: A 7-year-old girl with a history of amblyopia presented with acute onset of painless bilateral mydriasis (7.0-7.5 mm) and absent light and accommodation reflexes persisting for 7 days, following resolution of a mild upper respiratory infection one week prior. Initial neurological examination showed normoactive deep tendon reflexes, normal strength (grade V throughout), normal gait and coordination, and intact cranial nerves. Ophthalmologic examination revealed bilateral fixed mydriasis unresponsive to light or accommodation but with preserved convergence reflex and full extraocular movements—an atypical presentation of Miller-Fisher syndrome with isolated autonomic pupillary involvement rather than classic ophthalmoplegia. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed no albuminocytologic dissociation and was antibody-negative, which is atypical for classic MFS. However, serum anti-GQ1b (IgM/IgG) and anti-GT1a (IgG) antibodies were positive by western blotting, confirming the diagnosis of Miller-Fisher syndrome. The patient was treated with IVIG 400 mg/kg/day for 5 days. Post-treatment, pupil diameter normalized to 3–4 mm with restored light reflexes within 5 days. At 6-month follow-up, there was sustained resolution without recurrence or development of classic MFS features.
